reason: The sources thoroughly corroborate Shepard's Mercury background, Apollo 14 mission hurdles, and his iconic lunar golf experiment with dual-site verification.
story: Ten years after becoming the first American in space, Alan Shepard commanded Apollo 14 to the Moon. Grounded for years by an inner-ear disorder, the 47-year-old astronaut fought his way back to flight status to become the oldest person to walk on the lunar surface. But Shepard had an extra mission in mind: lunar golf. After securing conditional permission from NASA management, Shepard attached a Wilson six-iron head to the handle of a lunar sample scoop. His rigid, pressurized spacesuit prevented a standard golf stance, forcing him to swing one-handed in the lunar dust. After striking two balls, Shepard famously proclaimed on live television that his second shot flew 'miles and miles and miles.' In reality, modern high-resolution photographic analysis revealed that his first drive traveled 24 yards, and his second reached roughly 40 yards. Even so, Shepard remains the only person ever to play golf on another world.
angle: Alan Shepard bragged on live television that his lunar golf shot flew 'miles and miles,' but photo analysis revealed his stiff one-handed swing sent the ball just 40 yards.

claims.claim: Alan Shepard became the first American to travel into space aboard Freedom 7 in May 1961.
Shepard was grounded from spaceflight due to Ménière's disease, an inner-ear condition that caused vertigo and nausea.
Following ear surgery in Los Angeles, Shepard was restored to flight status in May 1969.
Shepard commanded Apollo 14, which launched from Florida on January 31, 1971.
The Apollo 14 prime crew consisted of Alan Shepard, Stuart Roosa, and Edgar Mitchell.
At age 47 during Apollo 14, Shepard became the oldest person to walk on the Moon.
Before descent, the Apollo 14 Lunar Module guidance computer received false abort signals suspected to be caused by a loose ball of solder.
Apollo 14 achieved the third crewed lunar landing, touching down in the Moon's Fra Mauro region.
Shepard brought two golf balls and a six-iron club head to the lunar surface.
The improvised golf club was built by attaching the six-iron head to the handle of a lunar sampling tool.
The stiffness of the pressurized spacesuit forced Shepard to swing the golf club with only one hand.
After striking the second ball, Shepard exclaimed on broadcast that it went 'miles and miles and miles.'
Photographic analysis determined the first golf ball traveled about 24 yards and the second ball traveled about 40 yards.
The Apollo 14 astronauts collected approximately 94 pounds of lunar samples.
Shepard brought the modified club head back from the Moon and donated it to the USGA Museum.
The Apollo 14 command module splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean on February 9, 1971.

disputed: Whether the club was smuggled: popular lore claims Shepard snuck the club aboard, but primary records state he pre-cleared the stunt with MSC Director Bob Gilruth on the condition that all mission science was completed first. Scripts should state he cleared the demonstration rather than smuggled it.

The legend of Don Eyles being awakened from bed: popular accounts hold that MIT programmer Don Eyles was dragged out of bed to fix the LM abort code glitch, but Eyles affirmed this was a myth and he was already working in his office. Scripts should avoid the 'woken up in the middle of the night' narrative.
Exact launch second: Source S2 records launch at 4:03:02 p.m. EST, while S6 records 4:03:22 p.m. EST. Scripts should omit the precise second and state 4:03 p.m. EST.
